roots.name: A rule that works in one case works everywhere
roots.explanation: Students over-generalize a familiar rule, like bigger number means bigger quantity, or a single observation, into a universal law, ignoring units, position and context.

roots.name: An object's appearance or my own body defines its properties
roots.explanation: Students judge category, function or measurement by visual shape or personal standards, such as a handspan or a straight ruler, instead of by the underlying property.

roots.name: Quantities, rates and operations can be swapped freely
roots.explanation: Students ignore units and what a quantity means, so they confuse totals with rates, divide or add arbitrarily, and treat zero or negatives as impossible.

roots.name: A science word means what it means every day
roots.explanation: Students read technical terms like speed, heat or circular motion through everyday meanings, so precise scientific definitions get overridden.

roots.name: If I can't see it, it isn't there
roots.explanation: Students treat what they directly see as the whole truth and so deny unseen things or misplace seen ones, such as reflections and images.

roots.name: Bigger, thicker or more always means a stronger effect
roots.explanation: Students assume size, amount or distance scales directly with effect, ignoring other factors such as type, pole direction or what actually governs the outcome.

roots.name: Properties and forces are stuff that gets used up
roots.explanation: Students picture electricity, energy and forces as physical substances stored in objects, consumed in use, or needing contact to act.

roots.name: Natural is safe and good; extremes don't change things
roots.explanation: Students assume natural things are harmless or superior, treat biological parts like machines, and think extreme values merely scale a thing rather than changing its nature.

roots.name: One powerful person or center controls everything
roots.explanation: Students credit a single leader, ruler or organ like the brain with directly doing and creating all actions and rules, overlooking distributed systems.

roots.name: Light, cold and current flow like a fluid
roots.explanation: Students model invisible things such as light, cold, current and waves as liquids or gases that move, pour, bend, pile up or stop.

roots.name: Democracy simply means everyone votes and the majority wins
roots.explanation: Students equate political participation with equal voting and majority rule, missing representation, rights, organization types and accountability.

roots.name: Human senses and scales measure how the world works
roots.explanation: Students treat human perception and time scales as the standard, so they think we actively send out sight and objects actively produce or attract effects.

roots.name: Things happen only in the place where I see them
roots.explanation: Students tie phenomena and properties to a specific or extreme location, believing echoes, fields or materials behave differently or need special settings.

roots.name: Barriers and safety devices work by blocking or storing
roots.explanation: Students think protection means slowing, collecting or attracting the danger at a visible surface, rather than breaking a circuit or redirecting it.

roots.name: Past people were primitive and used things like us
roots.explanation: Students project modern purposes and assumed lower sophistication onto ancient people, structures and tools instead of reading them in their own context.

roots.name: The official or obvious reason is the only reason
roots.explanation: Students accept a single practical, legal or stated cause as the whole story and expect rules to change reality instantly.

roots.name: All governments and reformers are basically alike
roots.explanation: Students lump distinct political ideas, levels of government and reform goals together, ignoring differences in scope, election and aim.

roots.name: What feels or looks true in extreme cases is true
roots.explanation: Students trust personal feeling, popular belief or dramatic examples as proof and apply them as general rules.

roots.name: If it looks different, it has been destroyed
roots.explanation: Students equate visible change in form or appearance with loss or disappearance of the substance, or with a purely physical change.

roots.name: Harm has one familiar cause and one kind of victim
roots.explanation: Students see danger, help and damage through one narrow image, such as accidents, strangers or physical contact, and miss other causes and sufferers.

roots.name: Only big things matter, and big things never run out
roots.explanation: Students link importance and unlimited supply to large size, so they think small things lack properties and huge resources are infinite.

roots.name: Food comes from one source taken from outside
roots.explanation: Students believe nutrition and food security depend on a single food, input or total amount, ignoring varied nutrients and internal production.

roots.name: Visible signs of industry show who does what
roots.explanation: Students infer pollution, ownership, labor and success from the obvious picture, like smoke, owners or product quality, and miss the actual economic roles.

roots.name: Plants are either lifeless objects or like animals
roots.explanation: Students treat plants as passive things or as animals with intentions, so they misjudge dormancy, response, growth and body functions.

roots.name: Technology works like nature and always replaces the old
roots.explanation: Students map machines onto biology, assume new technology instantly beats old, and reverse cause and effect in natural processes.

roots.name: Historical roles and institutions were fixed and hereditary
roots.explanation: Students assume past positions, religions and groups were inherited, closed and unchanging, missing how societies varied and evolved.

roots.name: The stronger or more powerful side always wins
roots.explanation: Students equate strength, power or willpower with outcome, and assume interactions help only one side or benefit everyone.

roots.name: One medicine or treatment fixes everything similar
roots.explanation: Students blur prevention, symptom relief and cure, and expect a single remedy to work against every similar illness.

roots.name: Conflicts have one simple motive and a total winner
roots.explanation: Students reduce wars to a single universal cause and expect the winner to eliminate the loser quickly and completely.

roots.name: Poverty and disadvantage come from simple scarcity
roots.explanation: Students explain hardship by physical shortage or personal failure, and see oppressed groups as passive, ignoring social and structural causes.

roots.name: The obvious source creates or supplies everything itself
roots.explanation: Students credit one visible or central source with producing a result, ignoring that things are transformed or come from many contributors.

roots.name: Rulers, rank and wealth mean owning everything physically
roots.explanation: Students equate authority, rank or revenue rights with literal personal possession of objects, land or power.

roots.name: The visible carrier is also the source or cause
roots.explanation: Students confuse what carries something (particles, vehicles, animals) with what produces or moves it, and assume one simple path.

roots.name: Natural processes are single, uniform and happen everywhere simultaneously
roots.explanation: Students overlook regional variation, multiple sources and different timing in rivers, monsoons and landforms.

roots.name: The middle or straight-looking part is most important
roots.explanation: Students assume centers, straight lines and visible positions show the true intensity, motion or proportion, ignoring graph and geometry details.

roots.name: The past was simple, uniform and like today
roots.explanation: Students project modern borders, genders and single identities onto history, missing its diversity of people, groups and lives.

roots.name: Past worlds were documented, understood and like ours
roots.explanation: Students assume ancient societies left readable written records and the same surroundings as today, ignoring gaps and change.

roots.name: Everything behaves like water, simply and uniformly
roots.explanation: Students apply a single simple rule (flow loses energy, heat only speeds things up, liquids are like water) instead of recognizing varied behaviors.

roots.name: Things are simply harmful or harmless, all alike
roots.explanation: Students sort germs, chemicals, acids and animals into one danger category, ignoring that effects depend on type and context.

roots.name: Only the most obvious kind of value counts
roots.explanation: Students reduce wealth, labour, capital and motives to money or one narrow meaning, missing broader forms of value.

roots.name: Biological and work processes are simple, constant and the same for everyone
roots.explanation: Students assume sleep, work and rest are all-or-nothing, uniform across ages and fully reversible, ignoring variation and complexity.

roots.name: Power comes from one central source through one connection
roots.explanation: Students imagine a single link or central hub supplies everything, ignoring complete circuits, multiple roles and distributed parts.

roots.name: Visible effort or size shows real importance
roots.explanation: Students judge work, sectors and activities by how they look or are named, not by their actual definition, scale or contribution.

roots.name: Clean-looking means pure and all cleaning is the same
roots.explanation: Students equate cleaning, refining, treating and renewing with one simple removal of visible dirt, ignoring distinct processes.

roots.name: The most famous name began or caused everything
roots.explanation: Students credit well-known people, groups or events with starting or doing all, overlooking earlier, lesser-known or multiple contributors.

roots.name: Body parts work as simple single-purpose things
roots.explanation: Students treat organs as containers or lone actors with intentions, overlooking multiple parts, processes and cooperation.

roots.name: Trade is simple, local and one-sided
roots.explanation: Students picture exchange as only in markets, sellers' gain or single direction, missing wider networks and mutual benefit.

roots.name: Governments and policies always act fairly for the poor
roots.explanation: Students assume the state provides everything and acts benevolently, ignoring motives, other actors and unequal effects.

roots.name: My own culture, region or subject is the whole picture
roots.explanation: Students assume their own language, place or field is universal or dominant, overlooking diversity and links across areas.

roots.name: Feeling better or comfortable means the problem is solved
roots.explanation: Students use present comfort or absence of symptoms as proof that something works or is needed, ignoring hidden causes.

roots.name: Being available means everyone can access it equally
roots.explanation: Students confuse existence, openness or visibility of something with free cost, equal access or real control.

roots.name: One simple number or payment settles the whole matter
roots.explanation: Students treat a single payment, rate or instrument as the complete story, ignoring how interest, money and responsibility actually work.

roots.name: What I personally experience is true everywhere
roots.explanation: Students generalize from everyday local observations to all conditions, planets or situations, even when evidence differs.

roots.name: Waste, loss and change are always bad or useless
roots.explanation: Students see by-products and changes as only harmful or valueless, missing their roles and benefits in nature and industry.

roots.name: A thing does only one job or has one source
roots.explanation: Students assign each organism, hormone or food a single function or location, missing multiple processes and hidden sources.

roots.name: Things are either wholly good or wholly bad
roots.explanation: Students sort substances, signs and choices into pure good or bad, missing that balance, context and amount decide the effect.

roots.name: One factor alone decides the outcome
roots.explanation: Students focus on a single input such as quantity, seeds or ingredients, overlooking quality, purpose and supporting conditions.

roots.name: All institutions work alike and decisions are final
roots.explanation: Students merge different bodies and levels, such as courts, police and commissions, ignoring their separate roles and appeal processes.

roots.name: Bright, hot or dramatic means source or typical cause
roots.explanation: Students treat the most striking feature as the source or normal case, not distinguishing glowing from lit, or rare from usual.

roots.name: What exists now was always the original plan
roots.explanation: Students read present outcomes back into earlier intentions, ignoring how goals and reforms changed over time.

roots.name: Space things all look and work alike
roots.explanation: Students lump distinct space objects, missions and spacecraft into one generic template, ignoring that each differs in design, purpose and conditions.

roots.name: Technology works by simple, direct, magical connections
roots.explanation: Students ignore the hidden infrastructure, limits and one-way or layered links in communication systems, so they credit the visible device or assume universal two-way connectivity.

roots.name: A process stops where I stop seeing it
roots.explanation: Students treat the visible endpoint of a diagram, event or input as the true end, missing that processes continue, partly use inputs or leave lasting effects.

roots.name: Things are defined by looks, use, or location
roots.explanation: Students classify and explain industries, products and materials by surface features or convenience instead of by their underlying source, origin or real requirements.

roots.name: Pollution and waste simply vanish or stay put
roots.explanation: Students think harmful substances disappear or stay local when out of sight, missing that matter cycles, spreads and persists across places and time.

roots.name: Social rules and groups never change or break
roots.explanation: Students see social systems, classes and institutions as fixed, uniform and obeyed, overlooking change over time, exceptions, and varied individual choices.

roots.name: Powerful rulers acted mainly for everyone's good
roots.explanation: Students credit colonial authorities with benevolent motives and originating progress, overlooking their self-interest, and earlier local systems and varied motives.

roots.name: Strong opposing ideas must be extreme or negative
roots.explanation: Students reduce nuanced concepts to simple good-versus-bad or passive-versus-violent pairs, missing that firmness, feeling, or bias can be non-violent, positive, or subtle.

roots.name: What is advertised or visible is the truth
roots.explanation: Students trust brand names, ads and surface appearances as accurate descriptions of quality and operation, not seeing the larger hidden system behind them.

roots.name: Breaking or burning things only destroys them
roots.explanation: Students think heat, fire or division simply ends life, matter or harm, missing that they also transform matter, create new things and may leave contaminants intact.

roots.name: Disappearing means being destroyed or extinct
roots.explanation: Students equate absence, loss from one place, or a risk label with total destruction, ignoring movement, partial loss, graded risk and transformation.

roots.name: Words mean only their most familiar, narrow sense
roots.explanation: Students stick to one common meaning of terms like migration or reservation, missing that they cover broader cases, levels and conditions.

roots.name: A name or tool means what it seems
roots.explanation: Students infer a thing's category or purpose from its origin, label or surface cue, instead of its actual definition, processing, or function.

roots.name: Similar-looking things are really the same thing
roots.explanation: Students merge distinct problems or objects that share a theme or appearance, such as green areas or environmental issues, rather than separating their different causes and features.

roots.name: Proper things must be neat, simple, and uniform
roots.explanation: Students expect stable, regular or standard cases to be tidy and identical, rejecting valid examples that are irregular, varied, or flexible.

roots.name: History facts follow familiar, expected patterns
roots.explanation: Students fill gaps with plausible assumptions, such as native rulers, simple succession or leader-serving documents, rather than the actual, messier historical record.

roots.name: Women were always powerless and passive
roots.explanation: Students assume women were uniformly oppressed, incapable or merely recipients, overlooking their agency, leadership and varied roles across times.

roots.name: Failure means foolishness or complete failure
roots.explanation: Students judge any unsuccessful result as total and irrational, ignoring partial successes, careful planning behind it, and many possible causes.

roots.name: Rural people all share one simple situation
roots.explanation: Students treat village life as uniformly farming, landless or jobless, overlooking the variety of occupations, circumstances and kinds of unemployment.

roots.name: Work without visible ownership or pay has no value
roots.explanation: Students overlook effort, investment and useful roles of vendors, labourers, middlemen and unpaid workers because they lack shops, property or wages.

roots.name: Friendly messages meant for me are trustworthy
roots.explanation: Students think personal-looking or kind messages are real and relevant to them, while believing helpful services are for other people.

roots.name: A natural thing has only one simple source
roots.explanation: Students reduce fossils, rocks and soil to one familiar origin, missing the multiple materials, processes and influences involved.

roots.name: A whole group is as bad as its worst
roots.explanation: Students judge entire categories by their harmful members or famous bad news, overlooking the many useful or necessary members.

roots.name: Old, small, or handmade things are judged simply
roots.explanation: Students assign simplistic value to ancient or handmade objects, seeing them as childish, as money, or as better, without checking their true purpose.

roots.name: Past success guarantees winning every time
roots.explanation: Students assume a famous or successful champion or ruler always wins, mixing up titles, events and records with unbeaten status.

roots.name: Social problems end when conditions change
roots.explanation: Students believe progress, laws or city life automatically remove injustice, and that movements aimed at only one narrow goal.

roots.name: Partial change means complete absence or shutdown
roots.explanation: Students read seasonal, selective or neutral conditions as total absence, treating reduced activity or impartiality as all-or-nothing.

roots.name: Similar-looking things work identically
roots.explanation: Students assume paired or related objects, like coasts, mirrors or masks, behave or perform the same, missing their real differences.

roots.name: Media has one simple source, form and stance
roots.explanation: Students see media as funded only by consumers, being only television, or having to side with the government, ignoring its varied funding, forms and independence.

roots.name: Institutions and rights have unlimited, uniform reach
roots.explanation: Students overstate the scope of courts and rights, assuming they cover everywhere, everyone or all levels, and exclusively through one body.

roots.name: Different institutions and their rules are all the same
roots.explanation: Students lump distinct bodies, cards and wrongdoings together, missing that each has its own role, rules and rates.

roots.name: Money is a physical object kept safely somewhere
roots.explanation: Students picture money as stored notes or value held in a vault, not as a trusted medium of exchange that banks lend out.

roots.name: A tool has one fixed use and works perfectly
roots.explanation: Students think a tool's usefulness depends on being intact and on its famous purpose, ignoring adaptation and broader uses.

roots.name: Where something comes from defines what it is
roots.explanation: Students infer a material's properties or category from its location or extraction, such as being underground, instead of its actual nature.

roots.name: Holy or wise things have supernatural, unchanging powers
roots.explanation: Students treat spiritual status as granting magical or physical immunity, rather than separating moral or spiritual qualities from physical reality.

roots.name: Similar-sounding things from the past are the same
roots.explanation: Students conflate related materials or eras, assuming a familiar material was always dominant and that related materials are identical.

roots.name: Historical works had one narrow, obvious purpose
roots.explanation: Students assume art and writing from the past served only the religious or expected theme, overlooking social, personal and critical content.

roots.name: Opposing a bad ruler makes someone good or foreign
roots.explanation: Students reduce political conflict to simple heroes versus outsiders, ignoring that rulers and enemies can be complex and internal.

roots.name: Events and institutions stay local and neutral
roots.explanation: Students assume events affect only one place and that international bodies are fair and equal, ignoring global links and unequal power.

roots.name: New technology arrives first and benefits everyone equally
roots.explanation: Students credit one region with inventions and assume innovations instantly reached all people, ignoring origins and unequal access.

roots.name: Extremes or largest values define every term
roots.explanation: Students equate words like outermost, highest or most common with the biggest or tallest, confusing position, frequency and size.

roots.name: Official or progress projects are purely beneficial and fair
roots.explanation: Students assume authority-backed development helps all and harms none, overlooking costs, displacement and unequal treatment.

roots.name: A safeguard works completely and in isolation
roots.explanation: Students believe separation or filtering is absolute and size-independent, missing that real systems overlap, interact and have limits.

roots.name: Powerful organizations act for public good
roots.explanation: Students assume big companies are state-owned or driven by helping the host country, rather than by profit.

roots.name: Services always cost money and need experts
roots.explanation: Students assume every service or legal process involves fees or professional help, not recognizing free or simple options.

roots.name: Copies and records match or belong to the person
roots.explanation: Students assume a copy resembles the original exactly and that any printed proof is meant to be kept, ignoring its actual purpose.

roots.name: Objects serve only their obvious purpose
roots.explanation: Students see items like jewelry as merely decorative, missing their social meaning such as status or identity.

roots.name: One famous leader is behind everything in an era
roots.explanation: Students credit a single well-known figure with all achievements and texts of a period, ignoring other people and contributions.

roots.name: Extreme environments are empty and uniform
roots.explanation: Students imagine harsh places as barren and the same everywhere, missing their variety of life and landscape.

roots.name: Natural systems are fixed and do not change
roots.explanation: Students treat dynamic features as static lines, overlooking seasonal and regular movement.

roots.name: Different categories are really the same
roots.explanation: Students merge distinct named seasons or classes because they seem related, missing the defining differences.

roots.name: Old pictures of a country never get updated
roots.explanation: Students hold outdated views of a country's past dependence, not recognizing changed present-day abilities.

roots.name: Composite measures are just one simple measure
roots.explanation: Students reduce an index with several parts to its most familiar component, such as income.

roots.name: Group schemes run on outside help, not member effort
roots.explanation: Students see community organizations as charity, overlooking that members' own contributions fund them.

roots.name: Symbols that look minor do not change meaning
roots.explanation: Students treat notation like brackets as decoration, when it changes how an expression is read and evaluated.

roots.name: Each need has separate procedures with no shared option
roots.explanation: Students assume every service has its own separate contact, missing that unified or simpler systems exist.

roots.name: Checks apply only to the best or most visible
roots.explanation: Students think monitoring targets only top performers, when it is often random or widespread.

roots.name: A project's results are wholly from the host country
roots.explanation: Students assume a nation's mission uses only its own equipment, overlooking international collaboration and shared contributions.

roots.name: Machines last as long as we imagine
roots.explanation: Students assume devices work indefinitely, ignoring design limits and harsh conditions that bound their lifetimes.

roots.name: Systems are single units, not connected parts
roots.explanation: Students picture one device doing everything, missing that it is made of separate cooperating components.
